transcript:
[00:00] Danielle Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. we're going to run through Private VPC networking, PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS, and then tie it back to runtime performance (kv cache, batching, quantization). I'm Danielle from Redwood, with Marco Ruiz (SE) who will lead most of the runtime bits.
[00:18] Sanjay Patel: Hey all, Sanjay here, CTO at Aurelius. Lisa and Tom are on from platform. high level we want to understand the networking constraints for private deployments and how that impacts latency and throughput.
[00:30] Marco Ruiz: cool, agenda — quick architecture review, PrivateLink vs NAT tradeoffs, endpoint placement and security groups, DNS/resolution and split-horizon, then runtime implications: kv cache locality, batching windows, grpc/keepalives, model artifacts pull.
[00:50] Lisa Chen: one note: we have a locked-down egress policy, almost everything must go through a NAT gateway or through vetted interface endpoints.
[00:58] Marco Ruiz: ok that's common. we'll cover both options.
[01:05] Tom Reynolds: also trying to avoid any public IPs on instances or ENIs; requirement from compliance.
[01:12] Marco Ruiz: yep. we support two common patterns for Redwood Private: 1) data plane fully inside customer VPC with PrivateLink to control plane, 2) data plane inside customer VPC talking only to customer-managed endpoints (S3/ECR/GCR) and control plane via PrivateLink. PrivateLink is preferred if you want no NAT egress, since traffic stays on AWS backbone.
[01:35] Sanjay Patel: can you unpack PrivateLink a bit? how do we connect? is it cross-account?
[01:40] Marco Ruiz: sure. Redwood exposes an endpoint service (NLB-backed) in our AWS account. Aurelius creates an Interface VPC Endpoint (com.amazonaws.vpce) in your account/subnet; that creates ENIs in the subnets you specify. Cross-account acceptance is needed (we accept the connection on our side) — it's pretty standard. The benefit: traffic flows over AWS private network, no internet egress, lower jitter.
[02:05] Danielle Park: note that PrivateLink handles control plane traffic and metadata calls. For data plane (actual inference tokens) we usually keep that entirely in customer's VPC — we deploy our runtime as AMIs/containers into your subnets (private subnets) in the Private offering.
[02:20] Lisa Chen: wait is the runtime running in our account or in Redwood's account?
[02:23] Marco Ruiz: in the Private model we can run the runtime either as customer-managed (you run the agents/images in your account) or we can deploy into a dedicated account with peering/Transit Gateway. For strict compliance customers you run everything in your account.
[02:37] Tom Reynolds: if we run in our account, we'll need to pull model artifacts and Docker images. that usually requires S3/ECR access — will that require NAT?
[02:45] Marco Ruiz: good question. for S3 you should create a Gateway VPC Endpoint (com.amazonaws.<region>.s3) — that's gateway-type and doesn't need NAT. ECR has regional interface endpoints (and sts, ecr-dkr). alternatively many customers use an internal artifact proxy or pre-warm the images into an internal registry. but for minimal egress, use the relevant VPC endpoints.
[03:05] Sanjay Patel: ok. about subnets. where do we recommend placing the interface endpoints and runtime nodes?
[03:12] Marco Ruiz: interface endpoints (PrivateLink) require one subnet per AZ where you want endpoint ENIs. For runtime nodes we recommend private subnets (no IGW), spread across AZs for redundancy. Route tables should not send those subnets' traffic to IGW; they can egress via NAT if needed but recommended pattern is VPC endpoints for required services.
[03:35] Lisa Chen: DNS — our internal resolvers are using Route53 Resolver inbound/outbound rules. how do we handle split-horizon?
[03:42] Marco Ruiz: good point. PrivateLink endpoints create DNS hostnames that resolve to the ENI IPs in your VPC if you enable private DNS for the endpoint. If you want to keep a custom split-horizon, you should disable private DNS and manage CNAMEs in your internal zone. Also we recommend Route53 Resolver rules to forward certain zones to Redwood if needed, but for most deployments private DNS on the endpoint suffices.
[04:05] Tom Reynolds: is there any MTU or fragmentation issues? we run jumbo frames on our network.
[04:10] Marco Ruiz: we typically see MTU 1500 works end-to-end; ENIs and PrivateLink support jumbo frames in some environments but you'll want to validate. fragmentation can add latency for large payloads; we recommend keeping keepalive/streaming chunks under 64KB to minimize fragmentation.
[04:30] Sanjay Patel: switching to runtime: how does networking affect KV cache locality and latency?
[04:36] Marco Ruiz: KV cache is in-memory on the same host that's serving the model. so if inference happens on nodes inside your VPC, cache hits are local (sub-ms). The bigger latency vector is if we have to route requests to a control plane or a different AZ. So collocating request ingress and model workers in the same AZ reduces cross-AZ hops and improves latency and cache warmness.
[05:00] Danielle Park: that ties to batching too — small batching reduces latency but increases pressure on per-token cost. We can tune micro-batching and target latency SLOs. Marco, any recommendations for batch window given private network?
[05:12] Marco Ruiz: with stable low-jitter network (PrivateLink + internal subnets) you can safely set batching windows 8-20ms for low-latency use cases and up to 50-80ms for throughput-oriented workloads. If you're using multi-node sharded models, cross-node network performance matters more; aim for AZ-local placement to avoid cross-AZ bandwidth caps.
[05:38] Tom Reynolds: what's the observed network bandwidth usage for a 13B model at 32k context, say 10 rps with average output 200 tokens?
[05:46] Marco Ruiz: rough ballpark — token bytes vary but assume ~1KB per token with codec/overhead, 200 tokens ~200KB per response. at 10 rps that's ~2MB/s sustained plus overhead. The dominating cost is CPU/GPU rather than raw network, but network matters for KV syncs and remote K/V stores. For sharded KV across nodes you'll see inter-node traffic; prefer colocated NVLink-backed nodes for sharded heavy workloads.
[06:12] Lisa Chen: we also want to enforce security groups to be minimal — what ports are needed between load balancer, ingress, and runtime nodes?
[06:18] Marco Ruiz: typically we need ports for the model runtime API (gRPC/HTTP) — default TLS 443 or custom port with TLS. Health checks from NLB may need TCP/health-port. SGs should allow inbound from the NLB ENI SG or from the set of ALB/NLB source SGs, and inter-node comms should be allowed on the internal port range (we'll provide exact ports).
[06:40] Marco Ruiz: one caveat: when using Interface endpoints, SGs on the endpoint ENIs can be used to restrict which clients in your VPC can talk to the endpoint; make sure the SGs permit traffic from your runtime nodes to the endpoint.
[06:55] Danielle Park: let's talk about cross-account and IAM. do we need to open STS or use cross-account roles for runtime initialization?
[07:03] Marco Ruiz: you can do either. For customer-managed runtime we recommend using an IAM role in your account for the runtime to access S3/ECR and STS. For cross-account deployments we use a cross-account role assumption flow with short-lived credentials; ensure sts:AssumeRole and relevant resource policies are in place. Also, if you want no internet, make sure sts endpoints are accessible via VPC endpoints for STS in the region.
[07:30] Sanjay Patel: about model downloads and quantization — we plan to use int8/quantized models. does quantization change networking or cold-start behavior?
[07:38] Marco Ruiz: quantized models are smaller on disk so they reduce S3/ECR transfer time for cold start. However, cold-start time is dominated by disk I/O and model initialization on the GPU, not network. For warm pipelines, KV cache warmness is more important. We recommend pre-pulling and pre-warming kernels during deploy to hide cold starts.
[07:58] Tom Reynolds: any special firewall rules for streaming? we expect a few long-lived streaming connections per session.
[08:05] Marco Ruiz: streaming gRPC long-lived connections are fine; ensure idle timeouts on load balancers and firewalls are long enough (minutes) — many corporate firewalls kill idle tcp after 1-2 minutes, which can interrupt streaming. Use keepalive pings at the application layer (we do this by default).
[08:25] Lisa Chen: performance SLAs. can you share expected tail latencies inside a customer's VPC vs hosted API?
[08:32] Marco Ruiz: hosted API has lower median latency because it's optimized on our network and routing, but Private in-customer VPC can match median and tail if you follow best practices: AZ-local placement, PrivateLink for control plane, VPC endpoints for artifact access, and NLB in front of workers. Expect p50 ~ 20-60ms depending on model size and quantization, p95 depends on batching and contention — we can run bench to get precise numbers for your workload.
[09:00] Sanjay Patel: let's talk fallback — if an AZ goes down, how do we handle requests?
[09:05] Marco Ruiz: we recommend multi-AZ deployment with local KV caches per AZ and a global cold-store (S3). On failover we route to healthy AZs; cache cold-starts increase latency temporarily. We support sticky routing to preserve cache locality for sessions but can failover to reduce downtime.
[09:25] Danielle Park: any recommendations for route tables and NAT sizing? some customers hit high SNAT table exhaustion with many ENIs.
[09:33] Marco Ruiz: yes, SNAT ports limited per NAT instance; use managed NAT Gateways for scale or use interface endpoints to avoid NAT. If you need many outbound flows, consider a proxy egress solution (e.g., via a small fleet of egress proxies behind an ALB) so you control SNAT usage. Also monitor ephemeral port exhaustion.
[09:55] Tom Reynolds: On the Redwood side, do you require any inbound peering or specific IP allowlists?
[10:00] Marco Ruiz: for PrivateLink no allowlist is needed, just endpoint creation and acceptance. If you prefer we can also do TLS mutual auth over peered connections; some customers prefer static IP allowlists behind NLBs and we can provide those as well for dedicated setups.
[10:20] Lisa Chen: DNS again — if we enable private DNS on interface endpoints, do we get automatic rotation if Redwood migrates backend?
[10:27] Marco Ruiz: the PrivateLink private DNS name resolves to ENI IPs in your account; if we migrate service behind the endpoint the ENIs stay the customer's IPs but the endpoint maps to our service. There can be small DNS TTLs; we typically recommend TTL 60s for resilience.
[10:45] Sanjay Patel: curious about metrics and observability — what do you expose and how does that look inside our VPC?
[10:51] Marco Ruiz: we ship logs/metrics to our control plane by default, but for Private deployments we can push metrics to your datadog/prometheus via an agent or allow remote write. If you don't want outbound to our control plane, we can store and forward metrics to your endpoints via VPC endpoints. Audit logs (who called what) can be kept locally and we can ship a copy if you want.
[11:15] Danielle Park: let's cover a concrete checklist for Aurelius to prep a pilot — Marco, can you list minimal required infra?
[11:22] Marco Ruiz: yes — 1) create three private subnets across 3 AZs for runtime nodes, 2) create interface endpoints for Redwood PrivateLink in those same AZs (or at least one AZ for initial test), 3) create gateway endpoint for S3, 4) provide IAM role for runtime with S3/ECR access or setup VPC endpoints for STS/ECR, 5) security group that allows inbound from NLB SG and inter-node comms, 6) Route53 Resolver rules if you want custom DNS forwarding.
[11:50] Lisa Chen: timeline wise we can create the staging VPC this week.
[11:54] Sanjay Patel: what about cost impacts — NAT vs PrivateLink, do you have order-of-magnitude?
[11:58] Marco Ruiz: NAT Gateway has hourly + per-GB egress charges; PrivateLink has per-hour endpoint and per-GB processed. For high egress to S3 NAT is cheaper; for control-plane calls and small metadata PrivateLink is cheaper and safer because it avoids public egress. We'll produce an estimate for your expected throughput.
[12:20] Tom Reynolds: last question — are there any special kernel/tuning params for low latency? tcp keepalive, net.core.somaxconn?
[12:27] Marco Ruiz: yes small kernel tuning helps: increase somaxconn, tcp_tw_reuse, tune net.ipv4.tcp_rmem/wmem, enable TCP_CORK/TCP_NODELAY as appropriate. We'll provide a recommended sysctl profile. Also set ulimits for file descriptors; model servers open many sockets for inter-process comms.
[12:50] Danielle Park: ok, recap and next steps — Marco will share architecture diagram and sysctl/profile, Danielle will send SOC2 and runbooks, Lisa will provision staging VPC, Tom will inventory firewall rules. we'll schedule a benchmark next week.
[13:00] Sanjay Patel: thanks all, this was super helpful.
[13:02] Marco Ruiz: thanks, we'll follow up with a detailed doc and the checklist.
[13:05] Danielle Park: bye all.
notes: Call included deep-dive networking and runtime tie-ins; customer requires no public IPs and restricted egress. Action items agreed to provision staging VPC and run benchmarks.
